prompt: A_TM is the set of encoded pairs ⟨M, w⟩ where machine M accepts input w; HALT_TM is the set of pairs where M halts on w. To mapping-reduce acceptance to halting, you map ⟨M, w⟩ to ⟨M′, w⟩, where M′ runs M on its input and accepts if M accepts. What must M′ do when M **rejects**?

options.explanation: Rejecting is halting. Then M′ would halt on w whenever M halts, including when M rejects, so halting of the constructed machine would no longer imply acceptance by the original machine.
Accepting also halts, giving the same problem as rejecting.
Correct. Then M′ halts on w exactly when M accepts w, which is the equivalence the mapping reduction needs.
A mapping reduction may not assume the decider it is trying to prove impossible. f must be built from M alone.

workedExample:
Check each case of M on w:

```
M on w     M′ on w
accepts    accepts (halts)
rejects    loops
loops      loops
```

So M′ halts on w exactly when M accepts w:

```formula
⟨M, w⟩ ∈ A_TM  ⇔  ⟨M′, w⟩ ∈ HALT_TM
where
M: the given Turing machine
M′: the edited copy that loops instead of rejecting
w: the input string
⟨M, w⟩: angle brackets: one string encoding M and w
A_TM: the acceptance problem: pairs where M accepts w
HALT_TM: the halting problem: pairs where the machine halts on w
∈: is a member of
⇔: if and only if
In words: the map turns acceptance questions into halting questions with the same answer.
```

f is computable: it rewrites M's table so the reject state goes into an infinite loop. It never runs M.
